questions.statement: Many coastal cities are highly __________ to rising sea levels, meaning they could easily suffer severe damage if ocean temperatures continue to climb.

questions.statement: According to the first paragraph, what is the primary business advantage of the "fast fashion" model?
questions.context:
**The Fast Fashion Dilemma**
Fast fashion—the rapid production of inexpensive, trendy clothing—has revolutionized the retail industry. Brands like Zara, H&M, and Shein can design, produce, and distribute a garment globally in under three weeks. This model offers consumers affordable ways to participate in passing trends, democratizing style that was once exclusive to high-end runways.

However, the hidden costs of this convenience are devastating. The textile industry is currently the second-largest polluter of clean water globally. To keep prices abnormally low, manufacturing is outsourced to developing nations where labor laws are lax, leading to sweatshop conditions and poverty wages for garment workers, overwhelmingly women.

Furthermore, the environmental footprint is massive. Fast fashion garments are often made of synthetic, petroleum-based fabrics like polyester, which shed microplastics into the ocean with every wash. Because the clothes are cheaply made and quickly go out of style, consumers treat them as disposable. As a result, millions of tons of textiles end up in landfills or are incinerated each year.

The emerging movement of "sustainable fashion" seeks to combat this. It emphasizes buying fewer, higher-quality items, thrifting, and supporting brands that guarantee ethical labor practices and use organic or recycled materials. Yet, the question remains: can sustainable fashion scale up enough to become the norm, or will the addictive allure of a five-dollar t-shirt continue to dictate the market?

options.text: It uses only high-end, expensive runway materials. <!-- feedback: Incorrect. The text says it produces "inexpensive" clothing. -->

It significantly accelerates the journey of clothing from the design phase to global distribution. <!-- feedback: Correct. The text states they can "design, produce, and distribute a garment globally in under three weeks." -->
It relies exclusively on organic and recycled materials. <!-- feedback: Incorrect. This is the goal of sustainable fashion, not fast fashion. -->
It guarantees high wages for women in developing nations. <!-- feedback: Incorrect. The text explicitly mentions "poverty wages". -->

questions.explanation:
Pedagógica
This tests scanning for specific information. The student must link "rapid production" and "under three weeks" to the concept of accelerating the journey.

The report recommend reducing emissions immediately. <!-- feedback: The verb does not agree with the singular subject. -->
The report recommending reduce emissions immediately. <!-- feedback: The structure is incomplete. -->
The report has recommend reducing emissions immediately. <!-- feedback: The auxiliary and participle are incorrect. -->

questions.explanation:
Pedagógica
Formal written English requires correct agreement and verb structure.

questions.statement: Which statement is best supported by the set of passages?

options.text: Local action matters only when national governments fail. <!-- feedback: The passages do not limit local action in that way. -->
Public participation is more effective when information is clear and evidence-based. <!-- feedback: Correct. That idea connects the recurring emphasis on informed action. -->
Environmental issues can be solved without cooperation. <!-- feedback: This contradicts the idea of shared responsibility. -->
Online communication always guarantees community engagement. <!-- feedback: One passage explicitly questions that assumption. -->

questions.explanation:
Pedagógica
The strongest answer captures the shared logic across the passages.

---

questions.statement: Which sentence has the most appropriate register for a formal campaign email?

options.text: Hey everyone, just fix it now. <!-- feedback: The tone is too abrupt and informal. -->
We kindly invite residents to review the proposal and share feedback by Friday. <!-- feedback: Correct. It is polite, precise, and appropriate for a formal message. -->
You all better answer this soon. <!-- feedback: The wording is too aggressive. -->
Stuff has to change somehow. <!-- feedback: The language is vague and informal. -->

questions.explanation:
Pedagógica
Register questions test whether language fits the situation and audience.

---

questions.statement: Choose the option that best completes the paragraph: "The project began as a school initiative. ______, local businesses later joined and funded the expansion."

options.text: As a result <!-- feedback: Correct. The second clause presents a consequence of the first stage. -->
Instead <!-- feedback: That would suggest replacement, not development. -->
For instance <!-- feedback: The second clause is not just an example. -->
Likewise <!-- feedback: The relation is not parallel. -->

questions.explanation:
Pedagógica
The connector must show causal progression from one stage to the next.

---

questions.statement: What assumption does the author of the second passage seem to reject?

options.text: People are able to verify information carefully. <!-- feedback: The passage does not reject that possibility outright. -->
Popularity online is the same as reliability. <!-- feedback: Correct. The warning about misinformation challenges that assumption. -->
Citizens can learn media literacy skills. <!-- feedback: That would support, not contradict, the passage. -->
Digital tools can help public communication. <!-- feedback: The passage criticizes misuse, not all digital tools. -->

questions.explanation:
Pedagógica
The text questions the idea that visibility or repetition guarantees truth.

---

questions.statement: Which conclusion best integrates the three passages?

options.text: Communities improve public life only through expert intervention. <!-- feedback: The passages emphasize shared responsibility, not only expert action. -->
Sustainable change depends on informed participation, trustworthy communication, and local cooperation. <!-- feedback: Correct. It combines the central ideas without exaggeration. -->
Technology should replace all face-to-face civic spaces. <!-- feedback: The texts do not support that replacement. -->
Environmental action matters more than any social factor. <!-- feedback: The passages link environmental and social dimensions. -->

questions.explanation:
Pedagógica
A strong synthesis preserves the main contribution of each passage.

---

questions.statement: In policy discussions, the adjective "inclusive" most nearly means

options.text: limited to one social group <!-- feedback: That is the opposite of inclusive. -->
open to different people and perspectives <!-- feedback: Correct. Inclusive policies seek broad participation and access. -->
hidden from public review <!-- feedback: That meaning is unrelated. -->
focused only on short-term profit <!-- feedback: That does not match the term. -->

questions.explanation:
Pedagógica
The meaning must fit civic and social participation contexts.

---

questions.statement: Choose the best final sentence for an argumentative paragraph about local climate action.

options.text: So climate change is huge. <!-- feedback: The sentence is too vague to close an argument. -->
For these reasons, coordinated local measures can produce measurable environmental and social benefits. <!-- feedback: Correct. It closes the argument with a precise conclusion. -->
Maybe something good happens someday. <!-- feedback: The wording is too uncertain and informal. -->
And that is why weather exists. <!-- feedback: This does not conclude the argument logically. -->

questions.explanation:
Pedagógica
A strong concluding sentence restates the claim with precision and purpose.

---

questions.statement: Which evaluation of the passages is the most rigorous?

options.text: They are persuasive because they use emotional words only. <!-- feedback: A rigorous evaluation considers evidence and reasoning, not only tone. -->
They are persuasive to the extent that claims are supported by examples, data, and clear causal links. <!-- feedback: Correct. This criterion evaluates the quality of the argument. -->
They are correct because they agree with each other. <!-- feedback: Agreement alone does not prove validity. -->
They are weak because they discuss social problems. <!-- feedback: The topic does not determine argument quality. -->

questions.explanation:
Pedagógica
Critical reading evaluates how claims are justified, not just whether they agree.

---

questions.statement: What criterion best improves a final evaluation of a public-information text?

options.text: Checking only whether the topic is popular. <!-- feedback: Popularity does not measure quality. -->
Reviewing claims, evidence, and causal links together. <!-- feedback: Correct. A sound evaluation examines how the text justifies its message. -->
Accepting the text if it sounds technical. <!-- feedback: Technical language alone is not enough. -->
Ignoring the intended audience. <!-- feedback: Audience matters in public communication. -->

questions.explanation:
Pedagógica
A rigorous evaluation combines content, support, and communicative purpose.

---

questions.statement: Choose the best transition for a conclusion: "The proposal reduces waste and improves participation. ______, it deserves serious consideration."

options.text: For this reason <!-- feedback: Correct. The connector links the reasons to the conclusion. -->
Meanwhile <!-- feedback: That marker indicates simultaneity, not conclusion. -->
In contrast <!-- feedback: The sentence is not contrastive. -->
For example <!-- feedback: The second clause is not an example. -->

questions.explanation:
Pedagógica
The transition must signal that the conclusion follows from the previous reasons.

---

questions.statement: Ana _______ en una empresa de tecnología en Bogotá. Ella _________ sus tareas a las 8 de la mañana.

options.text: trabaja / comienza
trabajas / comienza
trabaja / comienza <!-- feedback: "Ana" es third person singular, entonces se añade -s al verbo en afirmativo -->
trabajo / comienzan <!-- feedback: "trabajo" es primera persona singular, no concuerda con "Ana" -->

questions.explanation:
Pedagógica
En presente simple, los verbos en tercera persona singular (he/she/it) añaden -s o -es. Como "Ana" es tercera persona singular, "trabaja" es la forma correcta. El error común es confundir con la primera persona o con formas incorrectas sin -s.

---

questions.statement: Los estudiantes no _______ la tarea en clase. Ellos la _______ en casa.

options.text: hace / hace
hacen / hace
hace / hacen
hacen / hacen <!-- feedback: Sujeto plural "Los estudiantes" requiere la forma base del verbo en negativo y la forma plural en afirmativo -->

questions.explanation:
Pedagógica
Con sujeto plural (they), el presente simple no lleva -s. En negativo se usa "do not" (don't) + verbo base. El error común es añadir -s incorrectamente a verbos con sujetos plurales.

---

questions.statement: ¿_______ tú _________ español todos los días?

options.text: ¿Hace / hablas
¿Hablas / hablas <!-- feedback: Para formar preguntas en presente simple con "you", se invierte el orden: ¿Do you speak...? o simplemente "¿Hablas...?" -->
¿Haces / hablas
¿Hablas / hablas

questions.explanation:
Pedagógica
Para preguntas en presente simple con segunda persona (you), se usa "do" como auxiliar: "Do you speak...?" En español, el orden invertido indica pregunta. El error común es usar "makes" o "does" incorrectamente.

---

questions.statement: ¿_______ su madre _________ en Cali?

options.text: Hace / trabaja
¿Trabaja / trabaja? <!-- feedback: Con third person singular (she), el verbo en pregunta puede ir al inicio sin auxiliar en español, o usar "Does she work...?" en inglés -->
Trabaja / trabaja
Hacen / trabaja

questions.explanation:
Pedagógica
En preguntas con third person singular (she), en inglés se usa "does" como auxiliar. En español, el signos de interrogación indica la pregunta. El error común es no reconocer que "hace" no es auxiliar correcto aquí.

---

questions.statement: Mi hermano _________ como ingeniero de sistemas y siempre _______ nuevos proyectos.

options.text: trabaja / inicia
trabajas / inicia
trabaja / inicia <!-- feedback: "Mi hermano" es third person singular, requiere -s en el verbo: "works" y "initiates" -->
trabajamos / inician

questions.explanation:
Pedagógica
Tercera persona singular (he/she/it) requiere verbos con -s o -es. El error común es omitir la -s con sujeto singular o añadirla con sujeto plural. La concordancia sujeto-verbo es fundamental.

---

questions.statement: Yo siempre _______ inglés por la mañana antes de _______ a clase.

options.text: estudio / ir
estudia / voy
estudio / ir <!-- feedback: "Yo" es primera persona, usa la forma base del verbo sin -s. Los adverbios de frecuencia van con presente simple -->
estudia / va

questions.explanation:
Pedagógica
Con primera persona (I) y segunda persona (you), el verbo no lleva -s. Los adverbios de frecuencia (always, usually, often) se colocan antes del verbo principal. El error común es confundir personas y añadir -s incorrectamente.

---

questions.statement: _______ el profesor de inglés _______ la tarea todos los días?

options.text: ¿Hace / revisa
¿Haces / revisa
¿Revisa / revisa? <!-- feedback: Con third person singular (the teacher = he/she), en inglés se usaría "Does the English teacher review...?" -->
¿Revisan / revisa

questions.explanation:
Pedagógica
En preguntas con third person singular en inglés, se usa "does" como auxiliar seguido de la forma base del verbo. En español, el signo de interrogación indica pregunta. El error común es usar "makes" en lugar de un verbo específico.

---

questions.statement: Sofía no _______ la alarma por las mañanas porque ella siempre _______ temprano.

options.text: activa / despertamos
activas / despierta
activa / despierta <!-- feedback: "Sofía" es third person singular, por lo tanto el verbo en negativo no lleva -s después de "does not" -->
activan / despierta

questions.explanation:
Pedagógica
En negativo con third person singular: "She does not (doesn't) wake up early". El verbo mantiene la forma base. El error común es confundir la forma del verbo con la del afirmativo.

---

questions.statement: Ellos _______ emprendedores exitosos. Su negocio _______ en el centro de la ciudad.

options.text: tienen / queda
tienen / queda
son / queda <!-- feedback: El verbo "to be" (ser/estar) tiene formas especiales: am, is, are. Para "ellos" se usa "son/son" -->
es / queda

questions.explanation:
Pedagógica
El verbo "to be" es excepcional: I am, you are, he/she/it is, we/they are. Para "ellos" (they) se usa "are" en inglés, equivalente a "son" en español. El error común es tratar "to be" como verbo regular.

---

questions.statement: Los lunes, mi hermana _______ clases de música _______ la tarde.

options.text: tiene / en
tiene / por
tiene / por <!-- feedback: "Por la tarde" indica tiempo generalize, mientras "en la tarde" indica momento específico. "Por" se usa con partes del día en presente simple -->
tengo / en

questions.explanation:
Pedagógica
"Por la mañana/tarde/noche" se usa para indicar tiempo generalize en acciones habituales. El error común es usar "en" indistintamente sin considerar el matiz de generalidad vs. especificidad.

---

questions.statement: Los profesores _______ mucho. Nosotros _______ mucho también.

options.text: trabaja / estudio
trabajan / estudio
trabajan / estudiamos <!-- feedback: "Los profesores" es plural (they), entonces el verbo no lleva -s. "Nosotros" es first person plural, usa "estudiamos" -->
trabaja / estudiamos

questions.explanation:
Pedagógica
La concordancia sujeto-verbo en presente simple requiere: plural subjects = verbo sin -s. El error común es añadir -s a verbos con sujetos plurales o viceversa.

---

questions.statement: Mi abuela siempre _______ arepas para el desayuno. Ella _______ ingredientas frescos.

options.text: hace / usa
hace / usa
hace / usa <!-- feedback: "Mi abuela" (she) requiere third person singular: "makes" (-s) y "uses" (-s) -->
hacen / usan

questions.explanation:
Pedagógica
Con third person singular, ambos verbos deben llevar -s: makes/uses. El error común es la inconsistencia: usar -s en un verbo pero no en otro cuando ambos corresponden al mismo sujeto.

---

questions.statement: ¿____ María _______ el vuelo a Bogotá mañana?

options.text: ¿Reserva / reserva? <!-- feedback: La pregunta "Does Maria reserve the flight...?" en español se transforma usando signos de interrogación sin cambiar el orden del verbo -->
¿Hace / reserva
¿Reserva / hace
¿Hacen / reserva

questions.explanation:
Pedagógica
Para preguntas con third person singular en inglés se usa "does" como auxiliar. En español, el orden puede mantenerse si los signos de interrogación indican claramente la pregunta. El error común es usar verbos genéricos como "makes" en lugar de verbos específicos.

---

questions.statement: La librería _______ a las 9 de la mañana y _______ hasta las 7 de la tarde. El dueño _______ libros de historia.

options.text: abre / cierra / ama
abre / cierra / ama
abre / cierra / ama <!-- feedback: Todos los sujetos son third person singular: la librería, (él), por lo tanto verbos en -s -->
abren / cierran / ama

questions.explanation:
Pedagógica
Tercera persona singular (she/it) requiere verbos con -s. La librería = it, el dueño = he. El error común es mezclar formas plurales con singulares o viceversa.

---

questions.statement: Los turistas _______ el café de la región. Ellas siempre _______ el clima cálido.

options.text: ama / disfruta
aman / disfruta
aman / disfrutan <!-- feedback: "Los turistas" (they) y "ellas" (they) son sujetos plurales que requieren verbos sin -s -->
ama / disfruta

questions.explanation:
Pedagógica
Los sujetos plurales (they) requieren la forma base del verbo sin -s. "Aman" y "disfrutan" son las formas correctas. El error común es usar third person singular forms con sujetos plurales.

---

questions.statement: La gente _______ al lago porque _______ cuidar el medio ambiente.

options.text: respeta / decide
respetan / decide
respeta / decide <!-- feedback: "La gente" es singular en español pero se trata como plural (they) en inglés. En español se mantiene singular: "respeta" y "decide" -->
respetan / deciden

questions.explanation:
Pedagógica
"La gente" en español es singular, por lo tanto "respeta" y "decide" son correctos. En inglés, "people" es plural y requiere "respect" y "decide" (sin -s). El error común es pensar que "gente" funciona como "people" en inglés directamente.

---

questions.statement: Carlos _______ escultura porque él _______ el arte prehispánico. Su trabajo _______ en museos internacionales.

options.text: estudia / ama / exhibition
estudia / ama / exhibition
estudia / ama / se exhibe <!-- feedback: "Carlos" (he) requiere verbos en -s en inglés. En español, "estudia", "ama" y "se exhibe" concuerdan con el sujeto singular -->
estudian / aman / se exhibe

questions.explanation:
Pedagógica
Tercera persona singular (he/she/it) en inglés requiere -s en verbos. En español, tercera persona singular no tiene marca visible en infinitivos. El error común es omitir -s en inglés o añadirlo incorrectamente.

---

questions.statement: Mis padres no _______ redes sociales. Mi madre _______ correos electrónicos todos los días.

options.text: usan / envía
usan / envía
usan / envía <!-- feedback: "Mis padres" es plural: "usan" sin -s. "Mi madre" es singular: "envía" con -s -->
usa / envía

questions.explanation:
Pedagógica
Sujetos plurales y singulares en la misma oración requieren formas verbales diferentes. "Usan" para plural (parents), "envía" para singular (mother). El error común es no mantener la consistencia o confundir los sujetos.

---

questions.statement: El café de Nariño _______ en las montañas. Los agricultores _______ el café manualmente.

options.text: se cultiva / cosechan
se cultiva / cosechan
se cultiva / cosechan <!-- feedback: "El café" (it) es third person singular: "is cultivated" (-s). "Los agricultores" (they) son plural: "harvest" (sin -s) -->
se cultivan / cosechan

questions.explanation:
Pedagógica
La voz pasiva en presente simple con third person singular usa "is/are + past participle". Sujetos plurales usan "are". El error común es no concordar el verbo auxiliar con el sujeto.

---

questions.statement: Los jóvenes colombianos _______ empresas innovadoras porque _______ cambiar el mundo. Ella _______ como líder de su comunidad.

options.text: crean / desean / destaca
crean / desea / destaca
crean / desean / destaca <!-- feedback: "Los jóvenes" (they) plural: "crean", "desean". "Ella" (she) singular: "destaca" con -s en inglés -->
crean / deseada / destaca

questions.explanation:
Pedagógica
Crear texto con sujetos mixtos requiere cambiar entre formas plurales y singulares. La coherencia gramatical es esencial para la comunicación clara. El error común es la inconsistencia en el uso de personas gramaticales dentro del mismo texto.

---

**End of Bundle**

questions.statement:
Read the following advertisement from a travel magazine:

"Discover the magic of Cartagena! Walk through the colorful streets of the old city, enjoy the crystal-clear waters of the Caribbean, and taste the delicious flavors of Colombian cuisine. Book your dream vacation today at www.cartagenaparadise.co"

What is the main purpose of this text?

options.text: To describe the historical importance of Cartagena's fort
To promote tourism in Cartagena <!-- feedback: The text uses persuasive language like "dream vacation" and "magic" to encourage people to visit Cartagena -->
To explain how to cook traditional Colombian food
To compare Cartagena with other Caribbean destinations <!-- feedback: The text does not make any comparison with other destinations -->

questions.explanation:
Pedagógica
This question tests the student's ability to identify the main purpose of a text. The advertisement clearly aims to persuade readers to visit Cartagena, using marketing language and listing attractions. The distractors represent common errors: confusing promotional text with informative historical content (A), misidentifying the topic of "Colombian cuisine" as the main focus (C), and assuming comparative structure when none exists (D).

---

questions.statement:
Look at this excerpt from the TransMilenio schedule at a station in Bogotá:

"Portal Norte - Station: Estadio
First bus: 5:00 AM
Last bus: 11:00 PM
Frequency: Every 4 minutes during peak hours
Alimentador connections available"

What time does the last Alimentador bus leave Estadio station?

options.text: Every 4 minutes
The text does not specify this information <!-- feedback: The schedule only mentions that Alimentador connections are "available" but does not specify their operating hours or departure times -->

questions.explanation:
Pedagógica
This question assesses the student's ability to identify information that is NOT present in the text. Students often assume they can infer details that aren't explicitly stated. Option C is a common distractor because they might confuse the "Last bus" information (11:00 PM) with the Alimentador schedule. Option B is a distractor testing confusion between frequency and departure times.

---

questions.statement:
Read the email from the Universidad de los Andes admissions office:

"Dear prospective student,
Thank you for your interest in our Engineering program. After reviewing your application, we have decided to move forward with candidates whose profiles more closely match our current institutional needs. We encourage you to apply again next semester and wish you the best in your academic journey."

What can be inferred about the applicant's status?

options.text: They have been accepted into the Engineering program
Their application was not selected for this period <!-- feedback: The phrase "move forward with candidates" and the encouragement to reapply indicates the applicant was not selected -->
They need to submit additional documents
They have been waitlisted for the program <!-- feedback: The email does not mention a waitlist; it suggests reapplying, implying rejection -->

questions.explanation:
Pedagógica
This question tests inferential comprehension. Students must read between the lines to understand that "moving forward with other candidates" means rejection. The formal, polite tone is designed to soften bad news, which can confuse students who mistake politeness for acceptance. Option D is a plausible distractor because waitlisting is a real possibility students might assume.

---

questions.statement:
A Colombian environmental organization posts on Instagram:

"🌍 Our planet is dying. People keep throwing trash on the streets. If we don't change NOW, Colombia will be a huge landfill. Share this post if you care about your country!"

Based on this post, what is the author's primary intention?

options.text: To inform citizens about proper recycling methods
To celebrate successful environmental policies in Colombia

To persuade people to share the post and raise awareness <!-- feedback: The explicit call to action "Share this post" combined with emotional language reveals the main goal is viral mobilization, not education -->
To recruit volunteers for beach cleanups <!-- feedback: There's no mention of volunteering or specific cleanup activities -->

questions.explanation:
Pedagógica
Students often confuse emotional appeals with informative intent. This question requires analyzing the rhetorical devices (dramatic language, call to action) to determine purpose. Option A is a plausible distractor because environmental topics often involve education. Option D might seem logical since environmental organizations do recruit volunteers, but the text provides no evidence for this specific claim.

---

questions.statement:
Read the following excerpt from an article about Colombian coffee:

"The Colombian coffee crisis of the 1990s forced many small farmers to **abandon** their lands and migrate to cities like Medellín and Bogotá. Without government support, they had few options but to seek new opportunities in urban areas."

The word "abandon" in this context most nearly means:

options.text: To destroy
To leave permanently <!-- feedback: In this context, "abandon" means to leave behind, often reluctantly. The farmers left their lands due to economic crisis, not to destroy them -->
To sell
To visit occasionally <!-- feedback: "Abandon" implies finality; visiting occasionally does not fit the context of migration -->

questions.explanation:
Pedagógica
Context clues are essential here. The sentence explains that farmers "migrated to cities" and "sought new opportunities," indicating they left their lands permanently due to crisis. Option A confuses "abandon" with destructive intent. Option C incorrectly assumes economic transaction. Option D contradicts the permanent nature of migration described.

---

questions.statement:
A food critic writes about a restaurant in the Zona Rosa of Bogotá:

"The restaurant 'Sabor Paisa' offers authentic Antioqueño cuisine in a cozy atmosphere. The portion sizes are generous, and prices are moderate for the neighborhood. However, service can be slow during weekend evenings, and reservations are strongly recommended."

If a student wants to celebrate a birthday at this restaurant with 10 friends on a Saturday night, what should they do according to the review?

options.text: Order for delivery since dine-in service is too slow
Expect to pay premium prices due to the location
Make a reservation well in advance <!-- feedback: The text explicitly states "reservations are strongly recommended," especially relevant for a large group on a Saturday -->
Request a different day since the restaurant is closed on weekends <!-- feedback: The review mentions slow service on weekends, not closure -->

questions.explanation:
Pedagógica
This question tests whether students can extract actionable advice from a review. The explicit recommendation to make reservations is the key information. Option A is a logical leap that ignores the context of a celebration. Option B contradicts "moderate prices." Option D misreads "slow service" as "closure."

---

questions.statement:
A patient reads the following instructions on a prescription bottle:

"Take one tablet by mouth, twice daily with food. Do not operate heavy machinery. Avoid alcohol. If side effects occur, contact your doctor immediately."

What is the purpose of this text?

options.text: To advertise a new medication to doctors
To explain how to prepare the medication
To ensure the patient uses the medication safely <!-- feedback: The warnings about machinery, alcohol, and side effects indicate the text's purpose is safety and proper usage -->
To describe the ingredients of the medication <!-- feedback: No ingredients are listed; the focus is on usage instructions -->

questions.explanation:
Pedagógica
Students may confuse prescription instructions with advertising (A) or preparation procedures (B). The safety warnings are the clear indicator of purpose here. Option D is a plausible error because people often assume medication labels list ingredients, but this label focuses on usage protocol.

---

questions.statement:
Read the synopsis from a Colombian streaming platform:

"In the biopic 'Colombian Star,' we follow the journey of salsa legend Celia Cruz from her humble beginnings in Havana to her rise as the 'Queen of Salsa.' The film explores her complicated relationship with her family, her struggles with the music industry, and her ultimate triumph at the Grammy Awards."

How is the information in this synopsis organized?

options.text: Problem-solution
Chronological sequence <!-- feedback: The synopsis moves from "humble beginnings" to "rise" to "ultimate triumph," following the natural timeline of Celia's life -->
Compare and contrast
Cause and effect <!-- feedback: No cause-effect relationship is presented; it's a life narrative ordered by time -->

questions.explanation:
Pedagógica
This question tests text structure recognition. The key words "beginnings," "rise," and "ultimate triumph" indicate a life trajectory. Option A is a distractor because while there are challenges, no explicit problem-solution structure exists. Option C might attract students who think the film compares Celia to other artists. Option D confuses narrative arc with causal logic.

---

questions.statement:
The weather forecast for the upcoming week in Medellín shows:

Monday: Sunny, 28°C
Tuesday: Partly cloudy, 26°C
Wednesday: Thunderstorms expected, 24°C
Thursday: Heavy rain, 23°C
Friday: Clearing, 25°C

What can be inferred about outdoor plans for Wednesday?

options.text: They will be perfect due to the warm temperature
They should be postponed due to expected thunderstorms <!-- feedback: "Thunderstorms expected" clearly indicates risky weather for outdoor activities -->
They will be cancelled because it will rain heavily
They will be better on Friday since it's the end of the week <!-- feedback: While Friday looks better, the question asks about Wednesday specifically, not about comparing days -->

questions.explanation:
Pedagógica
This question requires connecting weather data to practical decision-making. Students may overgeneralize "thunderstorms" as complete cancellation (C), or they might make a comparison that isn't asked (D). Option A fails to recognize that thunderstorms are dangerous regardless of temperature. The correct answer tests focused inference from Wednesday's specific forecast.

---

questions.statement:
An opinion piece in El Tiempo discusses the future of work in Colombia:

"While automation will eliminate some jobs, it will create many more. We should focus on retraining workers for the digital economy rather than resisting technological change. Our education system must adapt, or Colombia will fall behind other nations."

What is the author's main argument?

options.text: Automation is harmful to Colombian workers
Robots should replace all manual labor jobs

Education reform is necessary to prepare workers for automation <!-- feedback: The author concludes that education "must adapt" as the solution to the automation challenge, making this the core argument -->
Colombia is currently the most advanced nation in technology <!-- feedback: The text says the opposite; Colombia risks falling behind -->

questions.explanation:
Pedagógica
Students must distinguish between the problem acknowledged (automation) and the solution proposed (education reform). Option A inverts the author's balanced perspective. Option B is never stated. Option D contradicts the explicit concern about falling behind. This tests the ability to identify the central claim rather than peripheral observations.

---

questions.statement:
Read this excerpt from a travel blog about San Andrés island:

"OK, so I've been to many Caribbean destinations, and honestly, San Andrés is overrated. The beaches are beautiful, yes, but the tourist infrastructure is lacking, prices are highway robbery, and the local government seems indifferent to the chaos. I guess you get what you pay for—except you're paying a lot."

The author's tone can best be described as:

options.text: Neutral and informative
Enthusiastically promotional
Disappointed and critical <!-- feedback: The author uses negative evaluative language like "overrated," "highway robbery," and "chaos," showing clear disappointment -->
Humorously exaggerated <!-- feedback: While some frustration is evident, this is genuine criticism, not humor -->

questions.explanation:
Pedagógica
Tone identification requires analyzing word choice and attitude. The adjectives "overrated," "highway robbery," and "chaos" reveal negative evaluation. Option A is incorrect because the author clearly expresses personal opinion. Option B is the opposite of the text's sentiment. questions.statement:

Hasty generalization <!-- feedback: The economist draws a broad policy conclusion from limited statistics without considering other factors like economic conditions, education, or regional differences -->
Ad hominem attack <!-- feedback: No personal attack against individuals or groups is present in the argument -->

questions.explanation:
Pedagógica
This is a higher-order question requiring critical evaluation of argument structure. The fallacy here is assuming that statistics alone justify a policy priority without comprehensive analysis. Option A might confuse the statistical evidence with circular logic. Option B incorrectly identifies a cause-effect error when the issue is scope. Option D is incorrect because no attacks on individuals occur.

Urban schools have no challenges to overcome
Structural resource inequality limits rural student achievement <!-- feedback: The researcher explicitly connects unequal resources to unequal results, implying systemic inequity -->

Pedagógica

However, we acknowledge limitations: our ground truthing covered only 15% of affected areas, and our satellite resolution may miss small-scale clearing operations. Despite these limitations, we maintain that our findings accurately represent the overall trend."

The limited ground truthing coverage <!-- feedback: Only 15% ground truthing leaves 85% of the data unverified, significantly undermining confidence in the satellite findings -->
The time period examined
The comparison between protected and non-protected areas <!-- feedback: The comparison is a valid analytical approach; it does not weaken the study -->

questions.explanation:
Pedagógica
Students must evaluate which methodological limitation most seriously compromises conclusions. While the study acknowledges multiple limitations, the 15% ground truthing coverage is the most severe because satellite imagery alone, especially with resolution limitations, cannot provide complete accuracy. Option A is a standard scientific method. Option C's seven-year period is appropriate. Option D represents sound comparative methodology.

Technical Inference. Distinguishing between mathematical operation and human-like understanding in AI.

---

questions.statement: Based on the text, what would be the most effective way to "identify potential pitfalls" in a new AI system?

options.text: Running the algorithm faster to see if it makes mistakes. <!-- feedback: Incorrect. Speed doesn't reveal bias; quality of output does. -->
Hiring only the most expensive mathematicians to write the code. <!-- feedback: Incorrect. The text emphasizes diversity, not just cost. -->
Having people from different backgrounds test the system for unfair outcomes. <!-- feedback: Correct. This aligns with the "diverse group of developers" mentioned in the text. -->
Asking the computer itself if it thinks it is being biased. <!-- feedback: Incorrect. This is logically impossible as the computer doesn't have moral self-awareness. -->

questions.explanation:
Pedagógica
Applying Textual Evidence. Extending the author's logic to a practical scenario of system testing.

---

questions.statement: As robotics ____ more sophisticated, the boundary between human and machine labor is blurring.

options.text: become <!-- feedback: Incorrect. "Robotics" is treated as a singular field/subject, requiring "becomes". -->
becomes <!-- feedback: Correct. Present simple for a general trend with a singular subject. -->
have become <!-- feedback: Incorrect. Would require a plural subject. -->
are becoming <!-- feedback: Incorrect. "Robotics" is a singular noun in this context. -->

questions.explanation:
Pedagógica
Subject-Verb Agreement. Recognizing that fields ending in "-ics" are usually singular.

---

questions.statement: Some economists predict that by 2040, nearly 40% of current jobs ____ by automated systems.

options.text: will replace <!-- feedback: Incorrect. The "jobs" are not doing the replacing; they are being replaced (passive voice needed). -->
will have been replaced <!-- feedback: Correct. Future perfect passive used to describe an action that will be completed by a specific time in the future. -->
would replace <!-- feedback: Incorrect. "Predict that" usually leads to a "will" structure. -->
are replaced <!-- feedback: Incorrect. Doesn't match the future time marker "by 2040". -->

questions.explanation:
Pedagógica
Future Perfect Passive. Describing a completed state in the future where the subject is the recipient.

---

questions.statement: While this may increase productivity, it also ____ questions about how society will support those whose skills are no longer in demand.

options.text: rises <!-- feedback: Incorrect. "Rise" is intransitive; you don't "rise questions". -->
raises <!-- feedback: Correct. "Raise" is transitive and is the standard verb used with "questions" or "issues". -->
arises <!-- feedback: Incorrect. "Arise" is intransitive and usually used for situations starting to exist. -->
rouses <!-- feedback: Incorrect. This means to wake someone up or provoke strong action. -->

questions.explanation:
Pedagógica
Confusing Verbs (Rise/Raise). Selecting the correct transitive verb for the idiomatic expression "to raise questions."

---

questions.statement: ____ universal basic income is a solution remains a subject of intense debate.

options.text: If <!-- feedback: Incorrect. While common in informal speech, "Whether" is preferred in formal contexts for a subject clause. -->
Whether <!-- feedback: Correct. Used to introduce a noun clause that functions as the subject of the sentence. -->
That <!-- feedback: Incorrect. "That" would state a fact, but the context is a debate between possibilities. -->
Because <!-- feedback: Incorrect. Doesn't fit the sentence structure which requires a subject for "remains". -->

questions.explanation:
Pedagógica
Noun Clauses as Subjects. Identifying the correct word to introduce an alternative functioning as a subject.

---

questions.statement: Which of the following scenarios best illustrates the author's point about the value of diverse development teams?

options.text: A team of five experts from the same university who all have the same degree. <!-- feedback: Incorrect. This is a homogeneous team, which doesn't address the author's point. -->

A team with people from different countries and backgrounds who identify that a facial recognition system fails for certain groups. <!-- feedback: Correct. Their diverse perspectives allow them to see a flaw that a homogeneous team might miss. -->
A company that hires people from many backgrounds but doesn't allow them to see the source code. <!-- feedback: Incorrect. Diversity without participation doesn't solve the bias issue. -->
A developer who uses five different programming languages to build a system. <!-- feedback: Incorrect. Technical diversity is not the same as human diversity mentioned. -->

questions.explanation:
Pedagógica
Synthesizing Evidence. Applying a theoretical argument about diversity to a concrete scenario.

---

questions.statement: Based on the text, what is the most sophisticated argument against relying solely on "mathematical objectivity" in AI?

options.text: Math is too difficult for most people to understand. <!-- feedback: Incorrect. This is an argument about accessibility, not the validity of objectivity. -->

Math processes inputs correctly, but if inputs are products of historical inequality, the result will formalize that inequality. <!-- feedback: Correct. It acknowledges the math is logically "correct" but the outcome is biased due to data. -->
Computers are eventually going to become smarter than humans and lie to us. <!-- feedback: Incorrect. This is speculative fiction and not supported by the analytical tone. -->
Human intuition is always better than any algorithm. <!-- feedback: Incorrect. The text doesn't say intuition is always better, but that algorithms need better oversight. -->

questions.explanation:
Pedagógica
Evaluating Complex Arguments. Distinguishing between a simplistic rejection of technology and a nuanced critique.

---

questions.statement: Which sentence would most logically connect the current text to a new topic about government regulation?

options.text: In conclusion, everyone should just try to be nicer to each other. <!-- feedback: Incorrect. Too informal and doesn't lead into regulation. -->

While technical and team-based solutions are helpful, they may be insufficient without legal frameworks that mandate transparency. <!-- feedback: Correct. It acknowledges previous points and introduces the new topic of legal frameworks. -->
Governments usually don't understand how computers work. <!-- feedback: Incorrect. This expresses an opinion that doesn't facilitate a logical transition. -->
Many politicians are now using AI to write their speeches. <!-- feedback: Incorrect. This introduces a new topic but doesn't connect logically to "solving bias." -->

questions.explanation:
Pedagógica
Cohesion and Coherence. Identifying the most logical transition that maintains the thematic progression.

---

questions.statement: Which sentence expresses the concept of "algorithmic accountability" with the highest level of linguistic precision for an advanced level?

options.text: We need to make sure that we can blame the right people when a computer makes a bad choice. <!-- feedback: Incorrect. Too informal ("blame", "bad choice"). -->
It's important to have a way to explain how AI works so it doesn't do anything wrong. <!-- feedback: Incorrect. Simple vocabulary. -->

Establishing accountability necessitates a transparent architectural framework wherein the logic underlying automated decisions can be audited. <!-- feedback: Correct. Uses high-level academic vocabulary ("necessitates", "framework", "audited") and complex structure. -->
Computer scientists must be responsible for the things they build. <!-- feedback: Incorrect. Understandable, but lacks technical and formal precision. -->

questions.explanation:
Pedagógica
Linguistic Precision (Register). Selecting the option that uses advanced academic terminology to express a complex concept.

questions.statement: While globalization has facilitated ____ unprecedented exchange of ideas, it has simultaneously triggered fears of cultural homogenization.

options.text: a <!-- feedback: Incorrect. "Unprecedented" begins with a vowel sound, so "an" is required. -->
an <!-- feedback: Correct. Use "an" before a word starting with a vowel sound. -->
the <!-- feedback: Incorrect. "An unprecedented exchange" is the standard way to introduce a new instance of this phenomenon. -->
such <!-- feedback: Incorrect. "Such" would require "a" or "an" after it in this context. -->

questions.explanation:
Pedagógica
Basic article usage in an advanced context. Identifying the correct indefinite article based on phonological rules.

---

questions.statement: Many argue that the dominance of Western media ____ the unique traditions of smaller communities.

options.text: threat <!-- feedback: Incorrect. This is a noun, but the sentence requires a verb. -->
threatens <!-- feedback: Correct. Third person singular verb matching the subject "dominance". -->
threatening <!-- feedback: Incorrect. This form would require an auxiliary verb. -->
threatened <!-- feedback: Incorrect. Past tense doesn't fit the present-tense discussion. -->

questions.explanation:
Pedagógica
Subject-verb agreement. Recognizing the grammatical role needed in the clause.

---

questions.statement: However, others contend that local cultures are not merely passive recipients; ____, they often "glocalize" global influences.

options.text: Moreover <!-- feedback: Incorrect. Used for adding supporting information, not introducing a contrast. -->
Rather <!-- feedback: Correct. Used to introduce a statement that corrects or contrasts with the previous one. -->
Therefore <!-- feedback: Incorrect. This would imply the "glocalization" is a result of being passive. -->
In fact <!-- feedback: Incorrect. While it can emphasize a point, "Rather" is more precise for correcting a negative assertion. -->

questions.explanation:
Pedagógica
Cohesion and Contrast. Selecting the precise adverbial to introduce a corrective alternative.

---

questions.statement: ____ this process to be successful, a balance between global integration and local preservation must be struck.

options.text: For <!-- feedback: Incorrect. "For" would introduce a reason, but here we need to introduce a purpose for a subject. -->
In order for <!-- feedback: Correct. Used to introduce a purpose or requirement for a specific subject. -->
So that <!-- feedback: Incorrect. Needs to be followed by a full clause with a subject and verb. -->
Because of <!-- feedback: Incorrect. This indicates a cause, not a purpose. -->

questions.explanation:
Pedagógica
Purpose Clauses. Recognizing the structure required to introduce a necessary condition for a future state.

---

questions.statement: If governments ____ more robust policies for cultural heritage decades ago, the current state of diversity might be more stable.

options.text: implemented <!-- feedback: Incorrect. Third conditional requires "had implemented" in the if-clause. -->
had implemented <!-- feedback: Correct. Past perfect used in the if-clause of a third conditional sentence. -->
would have implemented <!-- feedback: Incorrect. "Would have" belongs in the result clause. -->
have implemented <!-- feedback: Incorrect. This belongs to the first conditional or present perfect. -->

questions.explanation:
Pedagógica
Advanced Conditionals. Applying the third conditional to analyze hypothetical past actions.

---

questions.statement: How does the "Digital Commons" differ from traditional physical commons?
questions.context: The "Digital Commons"—which includes open-source software, Wikipedia, and public data—relies on voluntary contributions. Unlike physical pastures, digital resources do not diminish when used; in fact, they often become more valuable as more people participate (the network effect).

options.text: Digital resources are much more expensive to maintain. <!-- feedback: Incorrect. The text focuses on the nature of consumption. -->
Digital resources do not run out when more people use them. <!-- feedback: Correct. The text states they "do not diminish when used." -->
Only physical commons are subject to government regulation. <!-- feedback: Incorrect. Not discussed in the text. -->
Digital commons are owned by large corporations. <!-- feedback: Incorrect. The text says they are "open-access." -->

questions.explanation:
Pedagógica
Comparative reading. Identifying the fundamental distinction between two types of "commons" described in the passage.

---

questions.statement: What does the "network effect" imply in the context of digital resources?

options.text: The resource will eventually break if too many people use it. <!-- feedback: Incorrect. The text says it becomes "more valuable." -->
The utility of the resource increases as the number of users grows. <!-- feedback: Correct. This is the definition of the network effect mentioned. -->
Only people with a high-speed internet network can access the data. <!-- feedback: Incorrect. This is a literal misinterpretation. -->
The resource is automatically protected by a security firewall. <!-- feedback: Incorrect. Incorrect and technical misinterpretation. -->

questions.explanation:
Pedagógica
Terminology in context. Understanding a specific digital term based on the provided explanation.

---

questions.statement: What is the primary "threat" to the digital commons mentioned in the text?

options.text: Individual users consuming too much data. <!-- feedback: Incorrect. This is the "traditional" tragedy, not the digital one. -->
People losing interest in contributing to Wikipedia. <!-- feedback: Incorrect. Not the "primary threat" (enclosure) described. -->
Private companies restricting access to open data for profit. <!-- feedback: Correct. The text describes "enclosure" by corporations. -->
A global lack of interest in open-source software. <!-- feedback: Incorrect. The text focus is on corporate exploitation. -->

questions.explanation:
Pedagógica
Identifying key threats. Distinguishing between traditional and digital challenges mentioned.

---

questions.statement: The word "parasitic" suggests that corporations:

options.text: Are helping the digital commons grow faster. <!-- feedback: Incorrect. Parasites take without giving back. -->
Benefit from a system without contributing back to its survival. <!-- feedback: Correct. This matches the definition of a parasitic relationship in this context. -->
Are suffering from computer viruses and malware. <!-- feedback: Incorrect. Incorrect and too literal. -->
Are the main creators of the ecosystems they use. <!-- feedback: Incorrect. The text says they use "public knowledge." -->

questions.explanation:
Pedagógica
Metaphorical Language. Decoding an adjective used to describe a socio-economic relationship.

---

questions.statement: Which statement best captures the author's tone toward large corporations in this context?

options.text: Admiring. <!-- feedback: Incorrect. The author uses negative terms. -->
Critical. <!-- feedback: Correct. The author highlights how corporations exploit the digital commons. -->
Neutral. <!-- feedback: Incorrect. The choice of words like "parasitic" is judgmental. -->
Uncertain. <!-- feedback: Incorrect. The author's position is clear. -->

questions.explanation:
Pedagógica
Tone Analysis. Identifying the author's critical stance through their choice of vocabulary.

---

questions.statement: The phrase "enclosure of the digital commons" is most likely an analogy for:

options.text: Deleting old files from a computer's hard drive. <!-- feedback: Incorrect. This doesn't involve restricting access. -->
Putting a fence around public land to charge for entry. <!-- feedback: Correct. This reflects the historical "enclosure" of physical pastures. -->
Building a faster internet network for schools. <!-- feedback: Incorrect. This is a positive development. -->
Encrypting personal emails to keep them private. <!-- feedback: Incorrect. Privacy is not commercial exploitation. -->

questions.explanation:
Pedagógica
Analogy interpretation. Connecting the digital concept back to its historical root mentioned in the text.

---

questions.statement: If the "network effect" were to fail, what would happen to a resource like Wikipedia?

options.text: It would become much more expensive to host on servers. <!-- feedback: Incorrect. Network effect is about value, not just hosting costs. -->
It would lose value and relevance as people stopped using it. <!-- feedback: Correct. Without users and contributors, the resource's value diminishes. -->
Large corporations would no longer be interested in it. <!-- feedback: Incorrect. Possible, but the primary impact is on the resource's own value. -->
It would automatically be converted into a physical book. <!-- feedback: Incorrect. Incorrect and illogical. -->

questions.explanation:
Pedagógica
Counterfactual Reasoning. Predicting the outcome of a scenario where a key principle is removed.

---

questions.statement: The gig economy ____ the labor market by offering flexibility to both workers and employers.

options.text: has revolutionized <!-- feedback: Incorrect. This option does not fit the grammatical or contextual requirements of the sentence. -->
has been revolutionizing <!-- feedback: Correct. Present perfect continuous emphasizes the ongoing nature of this change. -->
revolutionizes <!-- feedback: Incorrect. Present simple is less common for describing an ongoing transformation. -->
was revolutionized <!-- feedback: Incorrect. Passive voice doesn't fit here. -->

questions.explanation:
Pedagógica
Verb Aspect. Distinguishing between simple and continuous aspects to emphasize the ongoing nature of a trend.

---

questions.statement: However, this model often leaves workers ____ access to traditional benefits like health insurance.

options.text: without <!-- feedback: Incorrect. But "lacking" is more formal and stylistically advanced. -->
lacking <!-- feedback: Correct. A participle used to describe the state of the workers. -->
lacked <!-- feedback: Incorrect. Past tense doesn't fit the descriptive role. -->
lack <!-- feedback: Incorrect. Needs to be a participle. -->

questions.explanation:
Pedagógica
Participle Adjectives. Using a present participle to describe a state in a formal sentence.

---

questions.statement: ____ these challenges, many young professionals still prefer the autonomy of freelance work.

options.text: Although <!-- feedback: Incorrect. Must be followed by a full clause, not a noun phrase. -->
Notwithstanding <!-- feedback: Correct. A formal synonym for "Despite", followed by a noun phrase. -->
However <!-- feedback: Incorrect. Used to start a new sentence. -->
While <!-- feedback: Incorrect. Requires a full clause. -->

questions.explanation:
Pedagógica
Formal Prepositions. Recognizing "Notwithstanding" as a high-level formal connector for expressing contrast.

---

questions.statement: The question remains ____ governments can adapt labor laws quickly enough to protect workers.

options.text: if <!-- feedback: Incorrect. While common, "whether" is the standard formal choice for indirect questions. -->
whether <!-- feedback: Correct. Used to introduce a matter of doubt following "the question remains". -->
that <!-- feedback: Incorrect. Introduces a fact, not an inquiry. -->
which <!-- feedback: Incorrect. Doesn't fit the logical structure. -->

questions.explanation:
Pedagógica
Indirect Questions. Choosing the appropriate conjunction to introduce a noun clause of uncertainty.

---

questions.statement: Based on the author's logic, which would be the most effective strategy for protecting the digital commons?

options.text: Encouraging more individuals to write their own private articles. <!-- feedback: Incorrect. This doesn't address the "common" nature or the threat of enclosure. -->

Implementing "copyleft" licenses that legally require any derivative works to also remain open. <!-- feedback: Correct. This directly combats "enclosure" by ensuring that data remains within the public ecosystem. -->
Closing all open-access databases so that corporations have nothing to steal. <!-- feedback: Incorrect. This would destroy the commons itself. -->
Asking corporations to voluntarily promise that they will be nice to data. <!-- feedback: Incorrect. The author's use of "parasitic" suggests voluntary action is unlikely. -->

questions.explanation:
Pedagógica
Problem-Solving from Text. Identifying a strategy that logically addresses the specific threat (enclosure).

---

questions.statement: The author's use of the term "wrapped" in proprietary interfaces implies that the data is:

options.text: Being protected from hackers and cyber-attacks. <!-- feedback: Incorrect. "Proprietary" suggests a commercial restriction, not just security. -->
Being gift-wrapped and given back for free. <!-- feedback: Incorrect. The context of "profit" contradicts this interpretation. -->
Still present, but obscured or made inaccessible without a paid intermediary. <!-- feedback: Correct. "Wrapped" suggests a layer that controls access. -->
Completely deleted and replaced with lies. <!-- feedback: Incorrect. The text says they profit from the knowledge, so they wouldn't delete it. -->

questions.explanation:
Pedagógica
Decoding Figurative Language. Understanding how "wrapping" functions as a metaphor for restriction of access.

---

questions.statement: Which statement would most likely be a developer's defense against the "parasitic" accusation?

options.text: We don't actually use public data; we make everything ourselves. <!-- feedback: Incorrect. This would be a denial of the premise. -->
Being a parasite is the most efficient way to run a business. <!-- feedback: Incorrect. No developer would use such a negative term for themselves. -->

While we use open data, our proprietary interfaces provide the necessary curation that makes data usable for consumers. <!-- feedback: Correct. This provides a "value-added" justification for the "wrapping" process. -->
We believe that Wikipedia should be deleted. <!-- feedback: Incorrect. This is an extreme position that doesn't provide a logical defense. -->

questions.explanation:
Pedagógica
Perspective-taking. Identifying a plausible high-level defense for a practice criticized in the text.

---

questions.statement: Which sentence best uses advanced vocabulary to describe the tension in the "Digital Commons" text?

options.text: It's a big problem when companies take free stuff and sell it. <!-- feedback: Incorrect. Basic vocabulary. -->
The digital world is like a park where everyone can play, but some companies are building walls. <!-- feedback: Incorrect. Good metaphor, but less formal. -->

The salient tension lies in the dialectic between the non-rivalrous nature of digital assets and the mercantilist impulse to commodify the commons. <!-- feedback: Correct. Uses very high-level academic vocabulary to describe the exact issue. -->
If we don't stop corporations, we will lose all our free information. <!-- feedback: Incorrect. Simple structure and vocabulary. -->

questions.explanation:
Pedagógica
Linguistic Precision and Register. Identifying the most advanced and accurate academic summary of the conflict.

questions.statement: Select the best word for space (1):

options.text: transform <!-- feedback: Incorrect. Needs to be in the present perfect form (has + past participle). -->
transformed <!-- feedback: Correct. Present perfect "has transformed" describes a completed action with present relevance. -->
transforming <!-- feedback: Incorrect. "Has transforming" is ungrammatical. -->
transforms <!-- feedback: Incorrect. Third person singular present does not fit after "has". -->

questions.explanation:
Pedagógica
Verb tenses. Recognizing the present perfect structure for a transformative event.

---

questions.statement: Select the best word for space (2):

options.text: doubt <!-- feedback: Incorrect. This is a noun or verb, but an adjective is needed here. -->
doubted <!-- feedback: Incorrect. This suggests the potential is not believed, which contradicts the "revolutionary" context. -->
undoubted <!-- feedback: Correct. Adjective meaning "certain" or "not questioned," fitting the context of potential. -->
doubtful <!-- feedback: Incorrect. This would mean the potential is unlikely, which doesn't fit the sentence's logic. -->

questions.explanation:
Pedagógica
Word formation and Adjectives. Selecting the correct derivative to express certainty.

---

questions.statement: Select the best word for space (3):

options.text: Would <!-- feedback: Incorrect. While possible for hypothetical questions, "Should" is the standard modal for expressing ethical obligation or permission. -->
Should <!-- feedback: Correct. Used to ask about what is right or appropriate in an ethical debate. -->
Might <!-- feedback: Incorrect. Suggests a weak possibility, but the sentence is asking about societal permission. -->
Could <!-- feedback: Incorrect. Refers to ability, while the context is about moral permission. -->

questions.explanation:
Pedagógica
Modal verbs in ethical contexts. Distinguishing between ability, possibility, and moral obligation.

---

questions.statement: Select the best word for space (4):

options.text: will <!-- feedback: Incorrect. "Will" suggests a definite future, but the argument is a warning about a possibility. -->
could <!-- feedback: Correct. Used to express a potential future consequence or warning. -->
have <!-- feedback: Incorrect. "Interventions have lead" is ungrammatical (should be "have led" if present perfect). -->
are <!-- feedback: Incorrect. "Interventions are lead" is ungrammatical. -->

questions.explanation:
Pedagógica
Modals of possibility and warning. Identifying the correct verb to express a debated future outcome.

---

questions.statement: Select the best word for space (5):

options.text: reach <!-- feedback: Incorrect. "Unless" clauses usually use the present simple for future meaning, but it must agree with "consensus". -->
is reached <!-- feedback: Correct. Passive voice in the present simple used to express a condition in an "unless" clause. -->
will be reached <!-- feedback: Incorrect. "Will" is not used in "unless" clauses to express future conditions. -->
has reached <!-- feedback: Incorrect. "Consensus has reached" implies the consensus reached something else. -->

questions.explanation:
Pedagógica
Conditionals (Unless). Using the passive voice in a conditional clause to express a necessary requirement.

---

questions.statement: What is the primary concern of the critics mentioned in the text?

options.text: That gene editing is too dangerous to be used for therapy. <!-- feedback: Incorrect. The text doesn't say therapy is dangerous; it focuses on the shift toward enhancement. -->
That the line between treating diseases and improving traits is disappearing. <!-- feedback: Correct. The text says the distinction is becoming "increasingly fragile." -->
That genetic traits should be sold as consumer products. <!-- feedback: Incorrect. This is what the critics *fear*, not what they support. -->
That children will be born with too much intelligence. <!-- feedback: Incorrect. Intelligence is mentioned as a trait, but the concern is about the "commodification" and "optimization" process. -->

questions.explanation:
Pedagógica
Identifying central arguments. Recognizing the specific ethical tension described in the passage.

---

questions.statement: The word "fragile" in the first paragraph implies that the distinction is:

options.text: Very strong and stable. <!-- feedback: Incorrect. "Fragile" means the opposite of stable. -->
Weak and easily broken or ignored. <!-- feedback: Correct. A fragile distinction is one that is no longer clear or easy to maintain. -->
Physically dangerous. <!-- feedback: Incorrect. "Fragile" here refers to a conceptual boundary, not a physical object. -->
Newly discovered. <!-- feedback: Incorrect. The term refers to the strength of the concept, not its age. -->

questions.explanation:
Pedagógica
Vocabulary in Context. Understanding the metaphorical use of a common adjective in a philosophical debate.

---

questions.statement: In the context of the passage, "optimization" refers to:

options.text: Making a computer program run faster. <!-- feedback: Incorrect. This is the technical definition, but not the context of the passage (human traits). -->
The pressure to improve human traits to meet societal or economic standards. <!-- feedback: Correct. The text connects it to "consumer choices" and "biological products." -->
Finding the best way to recycle biological waste. <!-- feedback: Incorrect. "Biological products" refers to humans in this context, not waste. -->
Reducing the cost of genetic therapy. <!-- feedback: Incorrect. Optimization here is about the traits themselves, not the cost of the service. -->

questions.explanation:
Pedagógica
Semantic interpretation. Defining a term based on its application within a specific socio-economic argument.

---

questions.statement: What would be a consequence of the "permanent biological underclass" mentioned in the text?

options.text: Rich and poor people would finally be equal. <!-- feedback: Incorrect. The text says inequality would become "permanent" and "hard-coded." -->
Everyone would have the same DNA. <!-- feedback: Incorrect. The text implies a divide between those who are enhanced and those who are not. -->
Social inequality would be based on biological differences as well as money. <!-- feedback: Correct. It would be "no longer just socio-economic, but hard-coded into our DNA." -->
DNA testing would become free for all citizens. <!-- feedback: Incorrect. The text suggests that enhancements (and thus the divide) are only for those who can pay. -->

questions.explanation:
Pedagógica
Synthesizing textual evidence. Understanding the long-term societal implications of an unequal technological advancement.

---

questions.statement: What is the author's primary purpose in the text?

options.text: To provide a technical guide on how CRISPR works. <!-- feedback: Incorrect. There is very little technical detail; it is an ethical discussion. -->
To highlight the ethical risks of moving from genetic therapy to enhancement. <!-- feedback: Correct. The passage focuses on the concerns of critics and the potential for new types of inequality. -->
To encourage parents to optimize their children's DNA. <!-- feedback: Incorrect. The author uses critical language ("commodification", "parasitic", "fragile") to warn against this. -->
To argue that all forms of gene editing should be banned immediately. <!-- feedback: Incorrect. The text mentions the potential to "eradicate hereditary diseases" as a positive starting point. -->

questions.explanation:
Pedagógica
Author's Purpose. Identifying the main goal of the writing based on the choice of examples and tone.

---

questions.statement: The phrase "inequality... no longer just socio-economic" suggests that in the future:

options.text: Wealthy people will lose their money but keep their good genes. <!-- feedback: Incorrect. The text suggests they will have both. -->
Poor people will finally be able to afford genetic enhancements. <!-- feedback: Incorrect. The text warns that they *won't* be able to, creating the "underclass." -->

Biological advantages will be passed down through generations along with wealth. <!-- feedback: Correct. "Hard-coded into our DNA" implies a permanent, hereditary biological advantage for the wealthy. -->
DNA will be used as a new form of digital currency. <!-- feedback: Incorrect. This is a science fiction concept not supported by the text's focus on inequality. -->

questions.explanation:
Pedagógica
Inference and Synthesis. Understanding how a technological change can transform a traditional social structure.

---

questions.statement: Michael Sandel's argument about "life as a gift" implies that:

options.text: Life should be free for everyone. <!-- feedback: Incorrect. "Gift" here refers to the nature of our existence, not the cost of living. -->
We should accept ourselves as we are, rather than trying to "design" our traits. <!-- feedback: Correct. The "gift" perspective contrasts with the "consumer choice" or "optimization" perspective. -->
Parents should give their children genetic enhancements as a birthday gift. <!-- feedback: Incorrect. This literal interpretation contradicts the philosophical point about acceptance. -->
Doctors should not be paid for performing gene therapy. <!-- feedback: Incorrect. This is a confusion about the word "gift". -->

questions.explanation:
Pedagógica
Philosophical Interpretation. Understanding a specific author's stance on the nature of human life in the context of technology.

---

questions.statement: Select the best word for space (13):

options.text: innovate <!-- feedback: Incorrect. This is a verb, but an adjective is needed to describe "ways". -->
innovative <!-- feedback: Correct. Adjective describing new and original methods. -->
innovation <!-- feedback: Incorrect. This is a noun. -->
innovatively <!-- feedback: Incorrect. This is an adverb and would modify a verb, not the noun "ways". -->

questions.explanation:
Pedagógica
Word Formation. Selecting the correct adjective form to describe a new technological development.

---

questions.statement: Select the best word for space (14):

options.text: know <!-- feedback: Incorrect. Base form doesn't fit the reduced relative clause. -->
known <!-- feedback: Correct. Past participle used in a reduced relative clause ("which is known as"). -->
knowing <!-- feedback: Incorrect. Present participle would imply the process is performing the action of knowing. -->
knows <!-- feedback: Incorrect. Third person singular present doesn't fit the structure. -->

questions.explanation:
Pedagógica
Reduced Relative Clauses. Identifying the passive participle used for naming or identifying a concept.

---

questions.statement: Select the best word for space (15):

options.text: Despite <!-- feedback: Incorrect. Needs to be followed by a noun or gerund, but here it introduces a full clause with a subject and verb. -->
Although <!-- feedback: Correct. Used to introduce a concessive clause (Although + subject + verb). -->
However <!-- feedback: Incorrect. Usually starts a new sentence or follows a semicolon. -->
Therefore <!-- feedback: Incorrect. Introduces a result, not a contrast. -->

questions.explanation:
Pedagógica
Connectors (Concession). Choosing the correct word to introduce a contrasting fact that precedes the main point.

to get up <!-- feedback: incorrect, infinitive doesn't fit in this context -->

questions.explanation:
Pedagógica
La respuesta correcta es C porque con "I" en presente simple se usa la forma base del verbo sin terminación. Los distractores reflejan errores típicos: agregar "-s" innecesariamente, usar gerundio sin auxiliar, y usar infinitivo en lugar de la forma correcta.
